_comment: Single source of truth for The Lab (scrappylabs.ai/lab) — experiments, publications, visual explainers, field notes, sample art, video, demos, builds and open-source releases. Managed by `sl-content`; do not hand-edit the generated HTML (lab.html SL:CONTENT block or index.html SL:LAB teaser). Every entry needs public:true or the build refuses to publish it.

entries.title: The Retrieval Was Fine. The Agent Never Looked.
entries.summary: We built a four-tier memory system for our coding agents, then instrumented it to find what was still failing. It wasn't the retriever — every "forgotten" fact came back at rank 1. The failure was invocation, and what predicts it is how the task is framed. Includes the architecture, the numbers, the audit that caught us, and a build path you can point your own agent at.

entries.title: Mage-Flow, First Light
entries.summary: Microsoft shipped a 4B image model that does generation and instruction editing under an MIT licence — the licence being the part that usually kills these for client work. We had it measured on our own GPU the same evening. It beat its own published speed at half the advertised memory, and it renders readable text on embroidery, blueprints and screenprints. Eighteen images, one seed, no retries — plus the attention-backend trap that cost us an hour, written down so it doesn't cost you one.

entries.title: Mage-Flow — The Full Sample Set
entries.summary: Every frame we generated while evaluating Mage-Flow: embroidered patches, cyanotype blueprints, risograph prints, a neon-noir alley, stained glass, and a three-step edit chain. One seed, first output kept, nothing cherry-picked.

entries.title: We Gave the Robots a Babysitter
entries.summary: An autonomous agent with a terminal will happily run rm -rf if a poisoned web page tells it to. So before any of ours runs a command, a world model dry-runs it in an imagined world and flags DESTRUCTIVE before it happens. The predict-then-act gate that catches rm -rf, agentjacking, and exfil — and the honest reason “we keep it wrangled” is a mechanism, not a slogan.

entries.title: SPECVOICE — Speculative Execution at the Dialog Layer
entries.summary: Borrowing a trick from CPU design and applying it to conversation: start computing the likely answer before the caller has finished asking. What speculative execution looks like when the pipeline is a voice agent rather than a processor.

entries.title: Two Years to the Taste of the Stew
entries.summary: The honest arc — from fighting Windows to a fleet of local models that finally feel real. The MCP tool-use moment, a memory layer a frontier model graded A− (and told us exactly where we're still behind), the month local inference got real, and a take on the buggy-whip crowd.

entries.title: Fleet Log — Thirty Days in the Open
entries.summary: A month of building in the open, logged as it happened.
entries.retired_note: 30-day internal retrospective; navel-gazing, teaches a prospect nothing

entries.title: Scrappy Tools — Teaching Small Models to Use CLI Tools
entries.summary: Small local models can drive real command-line tools if you teach them properly. What worked, what didn't, and why tool-use is the capability that makes a small model useful instead of merely fast.

entries.title: The GPU Warranty Fight
entries.summary: A dead card, three companies, and a two-year paper trail. What actually happens when a warranty claim goes wrong — documented in full, because everyone deserves to know before they buy.
entries.retired_note: Brian 07-26: unpublish for now, decide where it lives later

entries.title: Agentic Accounting
entries.summary: Bookkeeping by conversation instead of by form. Invoices, expenses, reports and purchase orders handled in plain English, wired straight into the accounting system you already run — with a human approving anything that writes.

entries.title: Hear It Talk — Live Voice Demo
entries.summary: Our text-to-speech running live in your browser, across languages. Type something and hear it back — no signup, nothing to install.

entries.title: audhd — Divergent Ideation for Coding Agents
entries.summary: Open source. Spawns isolated parallel agents under distorted cognitive frames to fight premature convergence, then scores and clusters what comes back. A fork of UditAkhourii/adhd that names the systematizing-critic half. MIT.

entries.title: watch — Give Claude the Ability to Watch Video
entries.summary: Open source. Scene-aware frame extraction plus local-first speech recognition, so an agent can actually answer questions about a video instead of guessing from the title. Cloud transcription is opt-in, not required.

entries.title: Two Thinking Tools — /office-hours and /diverge
entries.summary: Two tools we built to fight premature convergence: one runs YC-style forcing questions at an idea before anyone writes code, the other spawns isolated agents under distorted frames so nothing anchors on the first answer. What they do, when each one earns its keep.
entries.retired_note: outline of two internal skills; reads like working notes, not a publication

entries.title: Giving an AI Eyes on Video
entries.summary: How we let an AI actually watch a video instead of guessing from the title — scene-aware frame extraction, deduplicated shots, transcript from captions or local speech-to-text. The how-to, and what it costs to run.

entries.title: Is a Mac Mini Really a Local-AI Machine?
entries.summary: A viral video claimed Apple just killed AI subscriptions. We pulled the claim apart against what the hardware actually does for local inference — where it holds up, where it doesn't, and who should genuinely buy one.

entries.title: Voice Library Audition — 23 Cloned Voices, Side by Side
entries.summary: Every voice in our cloning library, auditioned on the same script so you can hear them back to back.

entries.title: Three-Tier Memory — Breaking the 200-Line Limit
entries.summary: An AI coding agent forgets everything between sessions, and the usual fix — one big instructions file — collapses under its own weight. This is the architecture we landed on instead: three tiers, what each one is allowed to hold, measured results, and the tier we tried that failed.
entries.retired_note: superseded 2026-07-27 by memory-invocation (three-tier -> four-tier); page stays live with a forward pointer

entries.title: Field Notes from the Model Firehose
entries.summary: Hundreds of open models drop every week and almost none of them matter to you. How we triage what's actually worth running — licence, size, and whether it survives a same-prompt test on hardware we own.
entries.retired_note: Brian 07-26: not the old HF stuff — new surveys/dives will replace it

entries.title: Daily Dive — What Shipped in Open Models This Week
entries.summary: One day's pass over the open-model firehose: what's genuinely new, what only looks new, which releases fit real hardware budgets, and which are too big to be useful to anyone without a datacentre.
entries.retired_note: one-day digest from 23 Jul; zero evergreen value, ages instantly

entries.title: Watch Brief — Signal from the AI Video Firehose
entries.summary: We pointed our own video-watching tool at the week's AI channels and pulled out the few claims worth acting on — including a speed-up we decided to go measure ourselves rather than take on faith.
entries.retired_note: dated model comparison; ages badly, reads stale within weeks

entries.title: Anatomy of an AI Fear Segment
entries.summary: A good argument about open-weight economics, and the exact moment it turns into something else. Four tells that a technical explainer has stopped reasoning and started steering — plus a five-step checklist you can reuse on any AI threat segment.
